title: Fukuoka — ramen
intro: Ichiran and Ippudo are both HQ'd in Fukuoka and world-famous, but local sentiment (a local blogger's ranked top-10 explicitly excludes both as "overpriced," and multiple Q&A threads call them "sousaku" ramen outside Hakata's traditional lineages, largely ignored by residents) points elsewhere. Ichiran in particular draws a real queue at almost any hour. Worth a look at Ippudo's original 1985 Daimyo shop for the history if you're curious, but Shin Shin and Ganso Nagahamaya are the better bowls by local reckoning.

items.name: Shin Shin, Tenjin main store
items.closed: Disputed across sources (3rd Tuesday vs. Wednesday) — confirm on arrival
items.why: The locals' pick — an independent Fukuoka ranking of local ramen put it #1, ahead of the globally famous chains. Also one of the few well-regarded shops open past midnight.
items.crowd_tip: A good late-night stop after Tenjin yatai. Third-party platforms show a reservation option — worth a call ahead for a specific night.

items.name: Ganso Nagahamaya
items.how: Near the Nagahama fish-market area, a short taxi or bus from Tenjin/Hakata.
items.why: The actual 1952 originator of Nagahama-style tonkotsu ramen, not one of the many shops that later took the name. Only choice is broth strength/noodle firmness/scallion.
items.crowd_tip: The early open makes it a genuine post-yatai or early-morning option.

title: Fukuoka — yatai, motsunabe & mentaiko
intro: There is no "Mentai Park" (Kanefuku's mentaiko theme-park chain) anywhere in Fukuoka Prefecture, despite this being a commonly repeated claim — checked directly against Kanefuku's own site; its six locations are all elsewhere in Japan.

items.name: Yatai — Tenjin & Nakasu
items.why: Officially licensed and location-assigned by Fukuoka City. Tenjin is where residents actually eat — cheaper (≈¥100–200 less per ramen bowl) and more Hakata-ben than tourist chatter — while Nakasu is the livelier, more tourist-facing riverside scene, worth seeing for the atmosphere even if Tenjin is the better meal.
items.crowd_tip: Best windows are right at opening or ≈21:00 once the first dinner rush clears. Bring {{fact:local-essentials-1000}} notes — stalls often can't break a {{fact:local-essentials-10000}} bill.

items.name: 長浜屋台 がぶがぶ。, Nagahama yatai district
items.why: Residents largely skip the pricier, tourist-oriented Tenjin/Nakasu yatai (no walls/AC, no reservations, tourist-priced menus) for the Nagahama district's stalls — noticeably cheaper (≈¥500–700/bowl) and locally frequented. The row nearly died out but a "Nagahama Yatai Revival Project" reopened several stalls; this one is confirmed still operating.
items.crowd_tip: The most local of the trip's three yatai options (Tenjin, Nakasu, here) — go if the Tenjin/Nakasu evening leaves you wanting the quieter, cheaper version.

items.name: Maedaya
items.why: The local-favorite motsunabe (offal hot pot) pick — recurs independently across a Q&A thread, a 2026 locals' ranking, and a resident magazine mention, stronger convergence than any single other option found.

items.name: Ganso Motsunabe Rakutenchi, Tenjin Honten
items.why: The famous, easily bookable motsunabe alternative — local rankings still place it a respectable 3rd for flavor, so it isn't a pure tourist trap, just the bigger, easier-to-book name.

items.name: Fukuya's Nakasu Honten
items.why: Fukuya is the brand that invented commercial mentaiko, and this location stocks a honten-exclusive tin not sold elsewhere.

items.name: Kisuimaru
items.address: Inside Hakata 1-Bangai / JR Hakata City, B1F
items.hours: 7:30–23:00, breakfast menu 7:30–10:00 with all-you-can-eat mentaiko/rice/miso soup
items.how: Right at Hakata Station — zero transit cost.
items.why: The pick to eat mentaiko-forward — a strong early-departure-day option given the zero-transit location.

title: Fukuoka — Yanagibashi Market
intro: On the optional Dazaifu day trip (see Sights), swing back through Nagahama for Ganso Nagahamaya (above) rather than eating near the shrine itself — Dazaifu's approach street is built for the grilled-mochi souvenir crowd, not a real meal.

items.name: Yanagibashi Rengo Ichiba
items.hours: ≈8:00–17:00, though each stall keeps its own
items.how: ≈10 min walk from Watanabe-dori or Yakuin subway station, between Tenjin and Hakata.
items.why: Nicknamed "Fukuoka's Kitchen" — a genuine working public fish/produce market with small sit-down counters, off the standard Hakata/Tenjin/Nakasu circuit. Fukuoka Now, the city's resident/expat magazine, has independently featured it across multiple years as one of the city's most distinctive spots to see actual daily commerce rather than a tourist market.
items.crowd_tip: It closes Sundays and national holidays, so it only works on a weekday or Saturday — the Oct 19 (Monday) lunch slot in Days is deliberate. Stalls thin out well before the 17:00 close; go for an early lunch, not a late one.

title: Sapporo — jingisukan, miso ramen & Nijo Market

items.name: Jingisukan Daruma Honten, Susukino
items.why: Sapporo's signature charcoal-grilled lamb, a shared, drinking-friendly grill format. Founded 1954, its own sauce recipe, named as "the place" for jingisukan across multiple independent write-ups. Sapporo Beer Garden is the larger, more tour-group-scaled alternative if Daruma is full.
items.crowd_tip: ⚠ Address/hours not independently confirmed against an official page — call ahead to book for a party of 4 and confirm current hours.

items.name: Menya Saimi
items.why: Sapporo is the birthplace of miso ramen; this shop stands out for genuine local following (its recipe became a retail instant-ramen product) rather than just tourist-guide visibility — a single-source lead, worth a walk-by rather than a locked plan.

items.name: Nijo Market
items.why: Sapporo's classic seafood market, good for a morning uni/crab breakfast; no strong "locals go elsewhere instead" alternative surfaced, so treat it as the standard, reasonably reliable pick.

items.name: Soup Curry GARAKU
items.address: 2-6-1 Minami 3-jo Higashi, Chuo-ku (Presento Minami 3 Higashi 2 bldg, B1F)
items.why: Sapporo's most internationally known soup curry — a dashi-based broth built from ~30 ingredients and 21 spices, with a spice-level scale from 1 up to 40. Independent write-ups converge on this as the essential bowl.
items.crowd_tip: ⚠ No reservations — a ticket-number system kicks in when busy, and lines are reported long at both lunch and dinner. Suage+ (founded 2007, fried-chicken-forward) draws similar local loyalty with reportedly shorter lines — a real fallback.

items.name: gop no Anagura (gopのアナグラ)
items.why: Off the main Susukino/Ōdōri soup-curry circuit — spice-forward, minimal-dairy stock, with other soup-curry shop owners cited as regulars here. The shop's own description: "うちの味はマニアック" (our flavor is for the die-hards). The novel alternative if GARAKU's line is too long or the goal is the locals' bowl, not the famous one.

items.name: Ganso Sapporo Ramen Yokocho
items.hours: Varies by shop — most open lunch through late night
items.why: A 42m alley of ~17 independent miso-ramen counters, tracing back to a 1951 ramen row demolished in 1969 for Olympic-era road expansion and revived at this location in 1971. A browse-many-shops pick that complements Menya Saimi rather than replacing it.
items.crowd_tip: Crowded with visitors through the day; locals mostly show up late at night after drinking in Susukino.

items.name: Sapporo Central Wholesale Market Outer Market (Jogai Ichiba)
items.hours: Market ≈6:00–17:00 daily; restaurants generally open from 7:00
items.price: Seafood-bowl set meals vary by shop, roughly ¥2,000–4,000
items.why: A working, wholesale-adjacent market of ~60–80 stalls and eateries sourcing straight from the morning auctions next door — a larger-scale alternative to Nijo Market for a seafood breakfast, at the cost of being further from Susukino.
items.crowd_tip: Less tourist-branded than Nijo Market day-to-day, but still a known guidebook name — a genuine second option, not an undiscovered secret.

title: Sendai — gyutan, hiyashi chūka & the back-alley izakaya lanes
intro: For the 2 of you continuing past Nov 2.

items.name: Ryūtei
items.why: The actual restaurant where hiyashi chūka (cold ramen) was invented in 1937, adapting the Shanghainese dish liangbanmian — a distinctive fact for Sendai's food identity, usually reduced to gyutan alone.
items.crowd_tip: ⚠ Confirm it's still open and check current hours locally.

items.name: Tanyaki Ichiryu Honten (たん焼 一隆 本店)
items.why: Run by a direct disciple of Sano Keishiro, gyutan-yaki's originator — named repeatedly across local sources as the residents' pick over the station-front chain row.
items.crowd_tip: Limited daily quantity — a line forms before opening. Confirmed still operating.

items.name: Date no Gyutan Honpo, Aobajo
items.why: On the former Date-clan castle grounds — a distinct gyutan (grilled beef tongue) pick from the big station-area chains most visitors default to.

items.name: Kokubuncho, Bunka-yokocho & Iroha-yokocho
items.why: Sendai's drinking district and its retro Shōwa-era back-alley izakaya lanes — tiny 8–10-seat bars in former storage-warehouse buildings, repeatedly named across independent sources as the city's nightlife core most visitors miss entirely.

items.name: Genji Izakaya
items.why: A 200-year-old former warehouse building with genuine local following — one specific standout inside Bunka-yokocho.

items.name: Abe Kamaboko-ten, Main Store
items.area: Chuo, Aoba-ku — ≈10 min walk from Sendai Station
items.hours: ⚠ Not independently confirmed against an official hours page — check current hours before going
items.why: The originator of sasakamaboko itself — the bamboo-leaf-shaped fish cake takes its name from the Date family's "sasa ni suzume" crest, and this is the founding shop. A no-reservation stall lets you hand-grill your own piece on-site.
items.crowd_tip: A good stop woven into a Kokubuncho evening or a daytime walk near Aoba Castle.

items.name: Zunda Saryo, Sendai Station
items.hours: ⚠ Not independently confirmed — station-floor hours generally track train hours, roughly 8:00–21:00
items.why: Zunda (sweet edamame paste) is Sendai's other defining flavor beyond gyutan — this is the specialty shop for it. Right inside the station, so it slots into an arrival or departure day with zero extra transit.
items.crowd_tip: Can queue at peak travel times — a between-train stop rather than a sit-down destination.

items.name: Oyster Hut Matsu
items.area: Matsushima, beside the Michinoku Date Masamune History Museum
items.hours: ≈10:00–15:00 (subject to the shop's own announcements — confirm locally)
items.why: Miyagi's oyster season runs autumn through winter, and this hut lets you grill/steam your own at the table — a genuine seasonal pairing with the Matsushima Bay sight. 45-min time limit; +¥500 adds fried rice and miso soup.
items.crowd_tip: ⚠ Hours are reported as subject to change — confirm same-day if possible.
